h1: Condominium renovation on the building's terms
hero_sub: Full-unit condominium renovations across Miami-Dade and Broward, scoped from your declaration and as-builts, sequenced around elevator windows and work-hour limits, permitted and inspected to close-out. Licensed and insured general contractor, Lic. CGC1539072.
local_heading: The building is the second client
intro_paragraphs: At the high end in South Florida, a condominium renovation is rarely a cosmetic refresh. It is a unit taken to bare slab and rebuilt: new layout, new millwork, new mechanical, electrical and plumbing, new floors and doors, ceilings dropped and re-planned around structure that cannot move. The owners are people who bought the view, the floor plate and the address, then decided the interior was somebody else's taste. Some occupy the unit full time, some split the year between here and elsewhere, and many are buying and renovating before they ever move in.

What changes is everything outside the unit. Many high-rise slabs are post-tensioned, so nothing is cored, cut or heavily anchored until the slab is scanned and, where the building requires it, the engineer of record signs off; we coordinate the scan and the engineer rather than perform them. A fixture often cannot move because of drain slope against slab thickness, and the space below the slab is normally outside your unit boundary, so the honest options are furring the floor up or leaving the fixture where it is. Plumbing serving more than one unit is generally a common element, and where your unit boundary stops is set by the recorded declaration, not by a rule of thumb.

We scope from documents before we scope from drawings: the declaration, the house rules, the as-builts and the association's renovation package. We assemble whatever that package asks for — signed and sealed drawings, certificates of insurance naming the association, contractor registration and a work schedule — so it reads complete on the first submittal. The decision remains the board's. Tying into an existing stack generally means the riser goes down for the whole line, which the building schedules, often outside normal hours. From there it is a fixed written scope, a supervisor on site daily, corridor and lobby protection, inspections passed and permits closed.

The work concentrates where the towers are. In Miami-Dade that means Brickell, Miami Beach, Bal Harbour, Surfside, Bay Harbor Islands, Sunny Isles Beach, Aventura, Key Biscayne and Fisher Island; in Broward it means Hallandale Beach, Fort Lauderdale, Coral Ridge, Pompano Beach, Lauderdale-by-the-Sea and Hillsboro Beach. Each building writes its own rules, so the walk-through tells us more than the neighborhood does. For local detail, the permitting authority, the housing stock and how the towers there are built, read the area page for your address, then the service page for your scope: kitchen remodeling, bathroom remodeling, whole-home remodeling, outdoor living or permitting and compliance.
scope_heading: What we handle inside the unit
scope_intro: Every project begins with a fixed written scope built from your building's documents, not from a template. These are the pieces that recur in high-rise work.

scope_items.name: Slab-aware demolition
scope_items.desc: Demolition planned around what the slab will allow. Where coring or anchoring is proposed, the slab is scanned and, if your building requires it, the engineer of record signs off first.

scope_items.name: Declaration and as-built review
scope_items.desc: Before anything is drawn, we read the recorded declaration, the house rules and the as-builts to establish where your unit boundary stops and which lines are common elements.

scope_items.name: Wet-area and stack work
scope_items.desc: Kitchens and baths rebuilt against real drain slope, with riser tie-ins scheduled by the building for the whole line, commonly outside normal working hours.

scope_items.name: Floors and sound compliance
scope_items.desc: Underlayment specified as a compliance item, not a finish choice. Sound-transmission requirements for flooring assemblies start in the building code and are commonly raised further by your declaration or house rules.

scope_items.name: Association submittal package
scope_items.desc: Signed and sealed drawings, certificates of insurance naming the association, contractor registration and a work schedule, assembled to read complete on the first submittal. The decision is the board's.

scope_items.name: Building logistics and protection
scope_items.desc: Elevator reservation windows, debris out by cart where the building has no dumpster access, corridor and lobby protection, and daily work-hour limits honored without a reminder from management.

faqs.q: What drives the cost of a condominium renovation up or down?
faqs.a: Scope drives it first: a finish-level refresh and a full gut back to slab are different projects. After that, the building does. Moving wet areas means drain slope, furring and sometimes engineering. Riser tie-ins scheduled outside normal hours cost differently than daytime work. Elevator windows, cart-only debris removal and restricted work hours all stretch labor hours. Sound underlayment set by your declaration is a compliance spec, not a finish choice. We price from a fixed written scope after we have read your building's documents.

faqs.q: How long does a condominium renovation take?
faqs.a: Two calendars govern it, and only one of them is ours. The permit calendar runs on the building department's process, and the building's calendar runs on your board's meeting schedule, elevator availability, work-hour limits and the riser shutdown windows the building sets for the whole line. An association's approval package can also carry its own completion deadline. We build the schedule after the walk-through, once we know which of those constraints apply to your building, and we give you dates we intend to keep rather than a template.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit, and do I need board approval?
faqs.a: Usually both, and they are separate tracks. Whether a given interior scope needs a permit varies by scope and by building department, and older buildings may require pre-demolition survey work before permits are released; we establish both during the walk-through rather than after demolition is scheduled. Separately, most in-unit reconstruction needs the board's prior written consent, and the association may condition it on repair methods, contractor qualifications or the contract used. Approval timing is set by your declaration and your board's meeting calendar, not by statute.

faqs.q: What could stop the job once it starts?
faqs.a: Three things stop condominium projects more often than anything else: a board consent that has not been granted, a slab condition found after demolition, and a plumbing assumption the declaration does not support. We remove the first by submitting a complete package and waiting for the written decision before we mobilize. We remove the second by scanning before we cut. We remove the third by reading the declaration and the as-builts before a new plan is drawn. Surprises are usually just questions nobody asked early enough.

faqs.q: Who is on site, and who talks to my building?
faqs.a: A licensed general contractor runs the job and a supervisor is on site every working day, not a subcontractor rotation with a phone number. The same team handles the building side: elevator reservations, access lists, protection of the corridor and lobby your neighbors use, and the daily contact with management so the first your board hears of a problem is not from a complaint. PGX Builders Group is licensed and insured under Lic. CGC1539072, with 20-plus years and 150-plus remodels and additions behind it.

faqs.q: Can I move the kitchen or add a bathroom?
faqs.a: Sometimes, and the answer comes from two places rather than from the design. A line that serves more than one unit is generally a common element, and the recorded declaration defines where your unit ends, so relocation is a documents question, answered from the declaration and the as-builts. The second limit is physical: drain slope against slab thickness, because the space below the slab is normally outside your unit boundary. Some declarations also restrict where wet areas may sit relative to the unit below. We check all of it before a plan is drawn.
